t.3.70.1: Bṛhadaśva said: He swiftly passed over rivers and mountains, forests and lakes, like a sky-goer coursing through the sky.
t.3.70.2: Then, as the chariot was speeding along in this way, King Bhāṅgasvari, conqueror of enemy cities, saw that his upper garment had fallen.
t.3.70.3: Then, when his upper garment had fallen, the high-minded king, in his haste, said to Nala, "I will pick it up."
t.3.70.4: "Rein in these exceedingly swift horses, O man of great wisdom, until Vārṣṇeya fetches this cloth of mine," he said.
t.3.70.5: Then Nala replied to him: "Your garment has fallen far away; it has been left a full yojana behind, and it cannot be recovered by you again."
t.3.70.6: When Nala had spoken thus, then King Bhāṅgasvari, O king, came upon a fruit-laden Vibhītaka tree in the forest.
t.3.70.8: No one knows everything; there is no one who is all-knowing. Nowhere in any single person does knowledge reach its complete perfection.
t.3.70.7: Seeing Bāhuka, the king, in great haste, said to him: “Charioteer, behold my own supreme power in counting.”
t.3.70.9: Of the leaves and fruits on this tree, Bāhuka, and of those that have fallen here, there are one hundred and one more: one leaf more and one fruit more, Bāhuka.
t.3.70.11: Then Bāhuka leapt down from the chariot and said to the king: "You boast, O king, tormentor of foes, as if of something beyond my sight."
t.3.70.10: There are five koṭis of leaves on the two branches together; pluck its two branches, and also the other small twigs. From these two there are two thousand fruits and a hundred less five.
t.3.70.12: Then, O king, nothing in your reckoning will remain beyond direct perception: before your very eyes, great king, I shall count the Vibhītaka tree.
t.3.70.13: For I do not know whether it may be so or not. I will count its fruits while you watch, O lord of men; let Vārṣṇeya hold the reins of the horses for just a moment.
t.3.70.14: But Bāhuka, exerting himself to the utmost, said to him:
t.3.70.16: Soothing him, O delight of the Kurus, Ṛtuparṇa said: "You alone are the charioteer, Bāhuka; there is no other on earth."
t.3.70.17: It is through you that I wish to reach the Vidarbhas, O expert in horses. I have come to you for refuge; you ought not to create an obstacle.
t.3.70.19: Then Bāhuka said to him, "Having counted this vibhītaka tree, I shall go on to the Vidarbhas; do as I say."
t.3.70.18: I will fulfil your wish, whatever you ask of me, Bāhuka, if you reach the Vidarbhas today and show me the sun there.
t.3.70.20: As though unwilling, the king said to him, "Count it." He quickly got down from the chariot and cut down that tree.
t.3.70.22: O king, I have witnessed this most wondrous power of yours. I wish to learn that knowledge by which this is known, O lord of men.
t.3.70.21: Then, having counted them, he found the fruits to be exactly as many as had been stated, and, filled with amazement, he spoke these words to the king.
t.3.70.23: Then the king, eager to be on his way, said to him: "Know me to be one who knows the secret of the dice and is skilled in counting."
t.3.70.24: Then Bāhuka said to him, "Give me this science, and from me in turn receive the secret of horses, O bull among men."
t.3.70.25: Then King Ṛtuparṇa, because of the urgency of his business and out of desire for the knowledge of horses, spoke these words to Bāhuka: "So be it."
t.3.70.26: "Take, as you wish, this supreme secret of the dice; let your secret of horses remain with you as a deposit for me, Bāhuka." Having spoken thus, Ṛtuparṇa indeed gave the knowledge to Nala.
t.3.70.27: From the body of him who knew the heart of the dice, Kali came forth, continually vomiting from his mouth the sharp poison of Karkoṭaka.
t.3.70.29: Then Kali, his self freed from the poison, assumed his own form. Nala, the lord of the Niṣadhas, enraged, wished to curse him.
t.3.70.28: Out of that Kali, tormented by it, the fire of the curse came forth; by it the king had long been wasted away, no longer master of himself.
t.3.70.30: Kali, frightened and trembling, his hands joined in reverence, said to him: "Restrain your anger, O king; I shall give you supreme fame."
t.3.70.31: Long ago, when she was abandoned by you, the mother of Indrasena cursed me in her anger; since then I have been sorely afflicted.
t.3.70.32: O lord of kings, O unconquered one, I dwelt within you in great misery, burned day and night by the poison of the king of serpents.
t.3.70.33: And those men in the world who tirelessly praise you shall never have any fear that arises from me.
t.3.70.35: Then, O king, when Kali had utterly vanished, the king of the Niṣadhas, slayer of enemy heroes, freed from his fever, counted the fruits.
t.3.70.34: Thus addressed, King Nala restrained his own anger; then the frightened Kali swiftly entered the vibhītaka tree. But Kali, while he was speaking with the Naiṣadha, was not seen by anyone else.
t.3.70.36: Filled with supreme joy and with surpassing splendour, the radiant one mounted his chariot and set forth with swift horses. And the Vibhītaka tree became ill-reputed because it had been the abode of Kali.
t.3.70.37: With a delighted inner self, Nala urged on again and again those finest of horses, which flew up like birds.
t.3.70.38: That great-minded king set out, facing toward Vidarbha. And when Nala had gone on his way, Kali too went to his own home.
t.3.70.39: Then King Nala was freed from his fever, O lord of the earth; released by Kali, O king, he remained bereft only of his true form.
